intro: Valse triste, Op. 44 No. 1, was written for a theatre stage, in a scene where a dying woman dreams that she is dancing and Death is among the guests. In Judith Bokor’s 1925 recording the cello plays the long melody and the piano accompanies.

sections.label: A · Waltz theme, cello and piano
sections.mNote: The cello plays the melody over the piano’s three-beat accompaniment.

sections.label: B · Waltz melodies
sections.mNote: Related waltz melodies alternate with the dance phrases.

sections.label: A″ · Waltz theme returns, louder
sections.mNote: Cello and piano play the waltz in longer phrases.

sections.label: Coda · Three quiet chords
sections.mNote: The waltz slows into its last short phrases.

relations.label: The opening waltz returns quietly
relations.basis: The opening waltz links the contrasting waltzes and is recalled in the quieter central stretch of this cello-and-piano arrangement. That recurring role is described by Richard Dyer at https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste; the later excerpt lies in the withdrawal marked near 132 s. CENS diagonal mean 0.926, sustained 14 s, fixed pitch-class shift 0 semitones and time offset 143 s (cache/form/sibelius-valse-triste.txt, candidate 4; 0.5 s grid). These are matched excerpts, not complete section boundaries; timing has not been checked by ear.

cues.title: Opening, cello and piano
cues.text: The piano marks three beats in each bar, and the cello plays a longer melody across them. Sibelius begins with the bare rhythm of the waltz, Lento in 3/4, and the accompaniment sounds before the melody enters.
cues.evidence: Sibelius, Valse triste, Breitkopf & Härtel orchestral score, plate Part. B. 1853, p. 2: Lento, 3/4, accompaniment before the melody. Richard Dyer also describes this opening: https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste . This recording uses cello and piano.
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Incidental music for Kuolema, 1903
cues.text: In Arvid Järnefelt’s play Kuolema, an old woman dreams of a masked ball, and her partner turns out to be Death. Sibelius wrote the music in 1903 for this play by his brother-in-law.
cues.evidence: Richard Dyer, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note, describes the scene, the family connection and the 1903 incidental music. https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste

cues.title: Form: four linked waltzes
cues.text: Sibelius joins four related waltzes, and the opening waltz returns between them to link the longer melodies. In this arrangement the cello plays the melody and the piano plays the waltz accompaniment beneath it.
cues.evidence: Richard Dyer identifies four related waltzes, linked by the opening waltz, in his Boston Symphony Orchestra note. The cue describes the piece’s design across the surrounding passage. https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste
cues.how: About the passage as a whole.

cues.title: Concert première, Helsinki, 1904
cues.text: Sibelius conducted the concert première in Helsinki on 25 April 1904, and the piece was published separately that year. Its first title was Valse lente (“Slow waltz”), before it became Valse triste, the “Sad waltz”.
cues.evidence: Richard Dyer, Boston Symphony Orchestra programme note: Helsinki concert première, 25 April 1904, separate publication in 1904 and original title Valse lente. https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste

cues.title: The final three chords
cues.text: The dance slows, and the opening waltz returns in short phrases. Three quiet chords follow the end of the melody. In the orchestral score Sibelius gave these chords to four solo violins; in this arrangement cello and piano play them.
cues.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate Part. B. 1853, p. 11: Lento assai, followed by three pp chords for four solo violins. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/2d/IMSLP212006-SIBLEY1802.12357.ba00-39087008746275score.pdf . Richard Dyer describes the three-chord postlude at https://www.bso.org/works/sibelius-valse-triste .
cues.how: Placed from the score; the timing is approximate.

transitions.title: Lento assai and three closing chords
transitions.how: Sibelius marks the closing passage Lento assai, very slow. Short phrases from the opening dance return, then the melody stops and three quiet chords end the piece. The cello-and-piano arrangement keeps this short passage after the waltz.
transitions.evidence: Breitkopf & Härtel full score, plate Part. B. 1853, p. 11: Lento assai and three closing chords. https://ks15.imslp.org/files/imglnks/usimg/2/2d/IMSLP212006-SIBLEY1802.12357.ba00-39087008746275score.pdf . The precise arrangement used by Bokor is unidentified.

composer.born: 8 December 1865, Hämeenlinna, Grand Duchy of Finland
composer.epithet: Composer who took the horn theme of his Fifth Symphony from sixteen swans he watched circling over Ainola, and who worked on the symphony for four years.
facts: Wegelius in Helsinki, 1885–89; Becker in Berlin; Fuchs and Goldmark in Vienna
Ainola, Lars Sonck’s timber house near Lake Tuusula, from 1904
Swedish at home; Finnish at school and in Kullervo and Luonnotar
Seven symphonies, one violin concerto, tone poems, theatre music, songs and chamber music
composer.background:
In Vienna in 1891, Sibelius auditioned for the Philharmonic and failed. He wanted to be a violinist; the jury found him too nervous even for an orchestral post. He was twenty-five, studying composition with Robert Fuchs and Karl Goldmark, spending money he did not have at parties and going to as much of the city’s music as he could. After hearing Bruckner’s Third Symphony he thought its author the greatest living composer. In his lodgings during the same period he was studying the rhythms of the Finnish Kalevala.

He was born in Hämeenlinna in 1865, when Finland was a grand duchy of the Russian Empire. His father, a doctor, died three years later, leaving debts. At home the family spoke Swedish; at school Janne learnt Finnish. He played chamber music with his sister Linda and brother Christian, and in 1885 went to Helsinki, nominally to study law. He was soon spending his days at Martin Wegelius’s Music Institute, where he befriended Ferruccio Busoni and worked through quartets by Haydn, Mozart and Beethoven. He took his professional name from a dead uncle’s visiting cards, which he had found. “Jean is now my musical name,” he told Uncle Pehr on 31 March 1886. After Helsinki he studied with Albert Becker in Berlin, and then in Vienna.
